guideTitle: 6 Best Shoelaces for Running Shoes in 2026
metaDescription: Six replacement laces for running and walking shoes, from oval polyester to flat braided and an elastic lock system, with length and width advice.
introParagraphs: Running and walking shoes are built with thin, padded tongues and lots of mesh, so the lace has more influence on comfort than most people realize. A cord that is too thick presses on the top of the foot, one that is too slick works loose, and one that is too short leaves you with no room to adjust at the midfoot. Swapping the factory lace is a cheap upgrade that often fixes all three.

The six sets here cover the common choices. Puzeam, Handshop, UpUGo and Birch are oval or half-round polyester laces, which are a long-standing favorite on athletic shoes. VSUDO is a flat braided lace for sneakers that want a broader, cleaner look. Lock Laces is the odd one out, an elastic system that skips the bow entirely.

We evaluated them using the listings: width, shape, length options, pack contents and maker claims. The most useful thing is matching the length and width to your actual shoe, so each pick below states which numbers the maker gives and where you will need to measure.

products.name: Puzeam 2 Pairs Oval Athletic Shoe Laces, 1/4 Inch
products.description:
Puzeam's oval lace is the most balanced pick for a running shoe. The six millimeter half-round profile slides through the narrow eyelets common on road runners and sits low under a thin tongue. The listing calls the lace anti stretch and hard to loosen, which are the two claims that matter on a long walk or run, since a lace that elongates through the day slowly loosens the whole shoe.

The polyester is described as resisting fraying, stretching and fading, so the color you pick should hold up in the wash. Four laces come in the pack, which covers two pairs, and the maker lists more than thirty-three colors. That makes it easy to match the accent color on your shoes or to color-code a household's trainers.

Compared with the Handshop set, Puzeam is a pack of two pairs and lists a firmer anti-stretch claim, while Handshop is a single pair with more length options. Compared with UpUGo, you get fewer pairs but a more specific hold claim. Check your old lace before ordering, because the listing has several lengths and the wrong one is the main reason for returns.
products.bestFor: Daily runners and walkers who want a reliable oval lace in a handy two-pair pack.
pros: Oval profile threads narrow eyelets easily
Large color range for matching shoes
cons: Several lengths make ordering easy to get wrong
Looks thin on classic flat-lace styles

products.name: UpUGo 3 Pair Oval Shoe Laces, Half Round
products.description:
UpUGo sells the biggest pack in the group: three pairs of oval laces at forty-eight inches. The listing says seven length options are available, from 30 up to 72 inches, so the same product line covers a low-cut trainer, a trail shoe and a boot. The material is polyester, described as sturdy and simple.

That range of lengths is the point. A typical running shoe with six or seven eyelet pairs will often take a 40 or 48 inch lace, but a lower-cut shoe may want a 35 inch lace instead, and the listing lets you pick. Three pairs also mean you can replace the laces on three pairs of shoes, or keep a clean spare for washing.

The tradeoff is that the listing gives fewer performance claims than Puzeam, with no anti-stretch language, so you are relying on the polyester's general durability. It is the cheaper per pair choice, and it is a good option for a household that rotates sneakers. Next to Birch, UpUGo has more lengths but fewer shown colors.
products.bestFor: Households with several pairs of trainers who want a multi-pack with many lengths.
cons: Fewer color details in the listing

products.name: Handshop Half Round Shoelaces, 1/4 Inch Oval
products.description:
Handshop's strength is choice. The listing offers thirty-four colors across eight sizes, starting from a 24 inch (60 cm) lace aimed at kids' shoes or two to three eyelet pairs, and running up through 30 inch (76 cm) and beyond. The lace we looked at is 115 cm, about 45 inches, in black. It is polyester, six millimeters wide, with a soft, delicate texture according to the maker.

The soft feel is a comfort advantage over stiffer laces, since a gentler cord is kinder to the top of the foot. It is described as fitting fashion sneakers, athletic shoes, casual shoes, kids shoes and trail running shoes. The listing is for a single pair, so it is not the best value per lace, but you will find the right length more easily than with a shorter menu.

Compared with Puzeam, Handshop has more sizes and a softer feel but no anti-stretch claim and a single pair. Compared with VSUDO, it is a thinner, rounder lace. It is the one to pick when your shoes are unusual, such as a kid's trainer or an eight eyelet trail shoe, and nothing else in the lineup offers the length you need.
products.bestFor: Shoes with unusual eyelet counts that need an exact length.
pros: Eight lengths from short to long

products.name: Birch Oval Shoelaces, 1/4 Inch Half Round
products.description:
Birch is a straightforward oval lace with a strong color range. The listing offers twenty-seven colors in four lengths, the shortest being a 75 cm lace for small shoes and the one we looked at a 94 cm medium. The shape is described as oval, or semi-round, and a quarter inch wide.

The listing is spare on performance claims beyond shape and color, and it includes a warning that colors may vary slightly from the screen. That honest note is useful if you are matching a particular shoe. With only four lengths, the sizing decision is easier than on the multi-size Handshop menu, but you may land between sizes.

If you want a plain, no-nonsense replacement and your main concern is matching a shoe's accent color, Birch is a fine choice. If you want an anti-stretch promise, Puzeam is the better one. If you want three pairs, UpUGo is better value. It sits in the middle for relative cost and is a neutral recommendation for people who just want a better lace than the one that came in the box.
products.bestFor: Buyers who care mostly about matching the color of their running shoes.
pros: Honest note about on-screen color variation
cons: Few performance claims in the listing
Only four lengths may not fit exactly

products.name: VSUDO 54 Inch Flat Shoe Laces for Sneakers, 8mm
products.description:
VSUDO takes the opposite approach from the oval laces. It is a flat, eight millimeter braided lace, 54 inches or 137 centimeters long, sold in a white and a black listing. The maker says the strong braided construction supports durability, and the broad flat shape gives a cleaner, more classic sneaker look.

The extra width is a benefit when you want pressure spread over the instep, which many walkers prefer on long days, but it can crowd narrow eyelets. A fifty-four inch length is generous, so it suits shoes with seven or eight eyelet pairs, or higher tops. On a standard running trainer with six pairs you may need to trim a tail or tie a double bow to use the extra length.

Compared with Puzeam's six millimeter oval, VSUDO is wider and flatter and gives a very different look. Compared with Lock Laces, it is a conventional bow lace. It is a single pair and mid in cost, so it is the right choice when you want white laces to refresh a clean pair of sneakers and care more about appearance than anti-stretch engineering.
products.bestFor: Walkers who want a broad, clean white or black flat lace on casual trainers.
pros: Classic look in white or black

products.name: Lock Laces Elastic Shoelace and Fastening System
products.description:
Lock Laces is designed around a runner's problem: stopping to retie. The listing describes the original no tie lacing system, built for triathletes who need to move from bike to run quickly. The stretch fit conforms to the foot and the compression aims to reduce discomfort, so the shoe feels snug and even rather than pinched at the bow.

It turns lace-up tennis shoes into slip-ons, which is ideal for quick changes at the gym or the trailhead. The relative cost is the highest in this guide, because you are buying a fastener system and not a plain lace. It takes a few minutes to set up and trim, and it is best done before the first run.

Compared with the oval laces, Lock Laces removes the daily bow entirely but changes the feel of the shoe. If you like to fine-tune tightness at different points, a conventional lace such as Puzeam gives more control by zone. If you want to put your shoes on and go, Lock Laces is the reason to pay more.
products.bestFor: Runners who want to stop retying and are happy with a snug, even fit.
pros: Quick on and off for transitions

buyingCriteria.criterion: Lace shape on a thin tongue
buyingCriteria.explanation: Running shoes often have thin, flexible tongues, so a lace that is too fat presses on the tendons on top of the foot. Oval laces such as Puzeam and Handshop at six millimeters are the safe choice, while VSUDO at eight millimeters flat spreads load and can feel better for people who dislike pressure points. Try the lace through one eyelet before threading the whole shoe. If it drags, go narrower.

Length is the most common mistake with replacement laces. UpUGo lists seven lengths from 30 to 72 inches, Handshop lists eight starting at 60 cm, Birch lists four and VSUDO is 54 inches. Count the eyelet pairs, measure your old lace laid flat and pick the closest size. Too short leaves no room to adjust, and too long leaves loops that can be stepped on.

A lace that stretches during a long walk loosens the whole fit. Puzeam is the only pick that names anti stretch and hard to loosen, and VSUDO points to a strong braided build. Polyester laces generally resist stretch better than cotton. Lock Laces uses stretch on purpose, so it needs a lock to hold the position.

buyingCriteria.criterion: Pack size and cost per pair
buyingCriteria.explanation: UpUGo gives three pairs, Puzeam gives two, and the other three picks give one. If you rotate between several pairs of shoes, a multi-pack is the practical choice. Single-pair listings make sense if you want the exact color or length once. Think of the lace as a consumable: runners go through them every few months. A three pair UpUGo pack means a spare is always ready, and a two pair Puzeam pack covers a second pair of shoes at once. Single pair listings like Handshop or Birch are better when you already know the exact length and color you want.

Narrow eyelets and mesh tongues are common on road shoes. Oval laces glide through them and the soft polyester of Handshop is gentle on delicate materials. A flat braided lace like VSUDO is better in sturdier trainers with wider eyelets. If your shoes have a sewn gusseted tongue, avoid very stiff laces.

Laces take sweat, mud and washing. Puzeam describes its polyester as resisting fading, Birch warns about screen color differences, and white VSUDO laces will show dirt quickly. Choose darker colors for trail use and white only for city shoes. Wash laces in a mesh bag if you can. If you want to swap colors with the seasons, the Birch range of twenty-seven shades and the Handshop range of thirty-four make it cheap to refresh a pair of trainers without buying new shoes.

howWeEvaluated.title: Fit to a running shoe
howWeEvaluated.description: We checked width and shape against the thin tongues and narrow eyelets of running shoes. Puzeam, Handshop and Birch use oval profiles at about six millimeters, UpUGo uses a similar oval, and VSUDO goes flatter and wider. Picks matched to typical athletic shoes scored higher.

howWeEvaluated.title: Length choices
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared how many lengths each set offers. UpUGo has seven, Handshop has eight, Birch has four, and VSUDO has only 54 inches. Sets that let you match the exact length scored better because the right length is the biggest source of buyer error.

howWeEvaluated.title: Durability claims
howWeEvaluated.description: We read claims about stretching, fraying and fading. Puzeam makes the most specific stretch claim, VSUDO notes braided construction, and the others offer general polyester language. We treated all of these as maker claims and gave extra credit to the more specific ones.

howWeEvaluated.title: Pack value
howWeEvaluated.description: Pack contents were compared: three pairs for UpUGo, two for Puzeam and one each for Handshop, Birch, VSUDO and Lock Laces. Cost relative to what you receive shaped our final ranking.

howWeEvaluated.title: Convenience
howWeEvaluated.description: We also considered the no tie option separately. Lock Laces is the only elastic system here, and we judged whether its convenience justifies the highest relative cost versus ordinary laces.

cards.label: Oval
cards.text: Puzeam, Handshop, UpUGo and Birch use half-round oval cord, which slides through narrow eyelets and gives a compact, biting knot. They suit most road and trail running shoes. Choose oval if your shoes came with round or oval laces.

cards.label: Flat
cards.text: VSUDO is a wide braided flat lace that spreads pressure and looks classic. It suits casual trainers with wider eyelets and thicker tongues. Choose flat if you want a broader, cleaner look or your shoes came with flat laces.

howToChoose.note: In short, oval for performance shoes, flat for casual sneakers.

howToChoose.intro: Match the lace to the number of eyelet pairs.

cards.text: A lace that does not stretch and does not press into the top of the foot. Soft materials and a stable knot matter more than color.

faq.q: What type of lace is best for running shoes?
faq.a: Most running shoes come with flat or oval polyester laces, and oval ones like Puzeam are a safe replacement. They thread easily through narrow eyelets and hold a bow well. If you prefer a broader feel, a flat lace such as VSUDO works.

faq.q: How do I know what length to buy?
faq.a: Count the eyelet pairs and measure your old lace flat. UpUGo, Handshop and Birch all provide size menus, and the listings tell you the length of each option. Choose the closest size and avoid going too long. If you land between two sizes, the longer lace is usually the safer choice for a double knot on a 54 inch VSUDO style pair, while the shorter one is better for stairs and busy sidewalks, where a trailing loop is the bigger hazard.

faq.q: Can I use runner's lacing tricks with these laces?
faq.a: Yes. Oval laces such as Puzeam and Handshop slide well enough to try a heel lock, which uses the top eyelets to cinch the ankle and stop heel slip. The extra length on UpUGo's 48 inch pack gives you room for it. Flat braided laces like VSUDO grip more, so they can be harder to pull through but hold the lock better once set.

Yes. A thick or slick lace can press on the top of the foot or work loose over a long walk. A softer polyester lace such as Handshop reduces pressure, and an anti-stretch lace such as Puzeam stays tight.

faq.q: Are elastic laces good for running?
faq.a: They were designed for it. Lock Laces started with triathletes who needed quick transitions, and the compression fit is intended to spread pressure. Some runners prefer the zone-by-zone tension of a bow, so it comes down to preference.

faq.q: How often should I replace running laces?
faq.a: Replace them when they fray, stretch or no longer hold a knot, which is often earlier than the shoe itself. A multi-pack such as UpUGo makes it easy to keep a spare. Laces are a cheap part of shoe maintenance. When you swap them, check the tips as well, because a worn aglet makes threading frustrating and is usually the first part to fail on thin oval laces like Birch.
Polyester laces generally tolerate gentle washing in a mesh bag, and the listings describe resistance to fading. Avoid high heat in a dryer. White laces such as VSUDO will need washing more often.
